name: Trigger.dev

plans.name: Free
plans.note: Hard cap: tasks stop when the $5 monthly credit is used; no overage on Free. 5 team members max. Burst up to 2x concurrency across multiple queues.

plans.name: Pro
plans.note: 200 concurrent runs included; extra concurrency self-serve at $10/month per 50, up to an 800 extra-concurrency quota (1,000 total) before review. 25 seats included, then $20/seat/month. Overage on by default (billing limit default 'No limit').

plans.name: Pro + 800 extra concurrency (self-serve max)
plans.note: Pro $50 + 16 x $10 bundles of 50 extra concurrency = $210/month; 800 is the default extra-concurrency quota, higher on request. Intermediate steps: +$10 per 50.

caveats: Durable TypeScript tasks, not arbitrary interactive VMs; mode is alt. Billed allocated machine seconds when executing plus $0.000025/run.
Wait >5 seconds and parent waiting for subtasks are checkpointed and unbilled. No execution timeouts. Free 20 concurrency; Hobby 50; Pro 200 + $10/month per 50.
Extra Pro seats $20/month beyond 25; HIPAA BAA is add-on not an included plan fee.
Null values mean unknown, not free/unlimited. No model-token cost, tax or unverified ancillary charge included.
Native browser/device/task/credit prices with unknown CPU/RAM are deliberately non-priceable. Check regime before interpreting any partial resource estimate.

API rate limit 1,500 requests/min on all plans (raise on request, paid only); batchTrigger up to 1,000 runs per call; batch token bucket Free 1,200 burst + 100/10 s, Hobby/Pro 5,000 burst + 500/5 s per environment.

Waits: wait.for/wait.until >5 s are not billed, but the concurrency slot is held until 60 s into the wait. chat.agent keeps the machine warm (billed) for idleTimeoutInSeconds (default 30 s) after each turn before suspending.
Only production/staging/preview are billed; DEV runs execute on the developer's machine and are not charged.
MicroVM compute (Firecracker) is in invite-only private beta in us-east-1-next, staging only; same presets, all sizes capped at 1 GB disk during the beta; no separate price published.

fleet.tiers: Free Production 20, Hobby 50, Pro 200. Pro buys extra concurrency in dashboard; documented extra-concurrency quota 800, beyond which human review is required.
fleet.notes: Per-environment/task-run concurrency, not permanent machines. Burst across multiple queues/tasks can reach 2x base; single queue remains base-limited. Per environment (Nov-2025 changelog, authoritative over the stale docs/limits table): Free Production 20 / Staging 10 / Preview 10 / Dev 25; Hobby 50 / 25 / 25 / 25; Pro 200 / 100 / 100 / 25.

audit_2026_09_29.source: checked against the provider's live pricing and docs pages

snapshot_auto.quote: While waiting for a subtask or during a long programmed pause (e.g., `wait.for({ minutes: 5 })`), the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state, including memory, CPU registers, and open file descriptors.
snapshot_auto.note: Triggered by waits (subtask triggerAndWait, wait.for/until >= 60 s, wait.forToken, input-stream waits) and by chat.agent idling out (idleTimeoutInSeconds, default 30 s). Memory/process state included (CRIU); on the microVM runtime (private beta) it becomes a full Firecracker VM snapshot. Restored transparently when the wait resolves. Scope is a task run, not a general VM.

snapshot_on_demand.note: No user-facing snapshot/checkpoint object, restore-to-point or fork API; checkpoints are an engine-internal side effect of waits (you can force one only indirectly by waiting >= 60 s). Replays re-run from the payload, not from state.

own_agent_api.quote: `AgentChat` lets you chat with agents from server-side code. It works inside tasks (agent-to-agent), request handlers, webhook processors, and scripts.
own_agent_api.note: Provider's own harness: chat.agent (AI SDK-based, you define the agent). AgentChat.sendMessage() starts a run, streams output and sends follow-ups to the same run; Sessions give durable two-way streams; Management API lists sessions; MCP server to chat with agents. No first-party wrapper for Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode (only a Claude Agent SDK guide running inside a task).

harness_api.quote: `AgentChat` lets you chat with agents from server-side code. It works inside tasks (agent-to-agent), request handlers, webhook processors, and scripts.
harness_api.note: Provider's own harness: chat.agent (AI SDK-based, you define the agent). AgentChat.sendMessage() starts a run, streams output and sends follow-ups to the same run; Sessions give durable two-way streams; Management API lists sessions; MCP server to chat with agents. No first-party wrapper for Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode (only a Claude Agent SDK guide running inside a task).

secret_proxy.quote: When creating an environment variable, you can mark it as a **Secret**. Secret values are hidden in the dashboard and cannot be viewed after creation.
secret_proxy.note: Secrets are environment variables delivered to the task process (optionally synced from Infisical or via syncEnvVars build extension). No credential-injecting egress proxy.

isolation.quote: You can review the build output by running deploy with the --dry-run flag, which will output the Containerfile and the build output.
isolation.note: Tasks are built into a container image (Containerfile) and each run executes in an isolated container on Trigger.dev's managed infrastructure; no VM/microVM hypervisor is exposed to customers on the public product (a Firecracker microVM runtime exists only as an invite-only private beta per the card).

image_oci.quote: Customize the deploy build process with one config line in trigger.config.ts... Getting FFmpeg, Playwright, or Python into production is a one-line change, with no Dockerfile to write or maintain.
image_oci.note: Trigger.dev builds the container image for you from your task code plus declared build extensions; there is no API to start a task machine from an arbitrary customer-supplied Docker/OCI image.

docker_inside.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
docker_inside.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — tasks run as managed, non-privileged containers on shared infrastructure; no documented support for running Docker/containers inside a task.

nested_virt.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
nested_virt.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — container-based managed task runtime; no /dev/kvm or nested virtualization documented.

desktop.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
desktop.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — a durable TypeScript task/workflow platform, not a desktop/VNC/RDP product. Playwright's optional non-headless mode only spins up an internal Xvfb virtual display for debugging, not a user-facing desktop.

browser.quote: Use the playwright build extension to use Playwright with Trigger.dev. Automatically installs Playwright and required browser dependencies. Allows you to specify which browsers to install (chromium, firefox, webkit)
browser.note: Real Chromium/Firefox/WebKit browsers can be installed and driven from inside tasks via the built-in playwright/puppeteer build extensions.

computer_use.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
computer_use.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no screenshot+click computer-use API; only code-level browser automation via Playwright/Puppeteer extensions.

anti_bot.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
anti_bot.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no stealth/fingerprinting-evasion features documented for the Playwright/Puppeteer extensions.

captcha_solving.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
captcha_solving.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no built-in CAPTCHA-solving feature documented.

egress_ip_type.quote: Get 4x more concurrency on paid plans and static IPs with our new AWS regions, starting with us-east-1 and eu-central-1.
egress_ip_type.note: Static per-region outbound IP addresses on AWS infrastructure, listed on the dashboard Regions page; datacenter (AWS), not residential/mobile.

ssh.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
ssh.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — ephemeral managed task containers triggered by events/API calls, not machines you SSH into.

snapshot.quote: the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state, including memory, CPU registers, and open file descriptors.
snapshot.note: Automatic checkpoint/restore during waits captures full process memory state; scoped to a task run (not a general-purpose VM snapshot).

fork.quote: the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state
fork.note: No API to clone a machine/run into new independent runs; checkpoints are engine-internal (used only to resume the same run), and replays re-execute from the original payload rather than forking saved state.

fork_running.quote: the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state
fork_running.note: No fork capability exists at all (see fork), so cloning a running machine without stopping it is not offered.

memory_snapshot_fork.quote: the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state
memory_snapshot_fork.note: CRIU checkpoints restore the same run in place; there is no fork-into-new-machine feature that would carry the in-memory state into a new, separate running instance.

wake_on_request.quote: Every conversation gets its own computer: it sleeps when nobody is typing so you stop paying for it, and wakes on the exact line of code it stopped on with the whole conversation still in context.
wake_on_request.note: chat.agent conversations (and general task waits) checkpoint/sleep and resume automatically when the next message/event arrives, with no separate wake call needed.

volume_attach.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
volume_attach.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — stateless task containers with a fixed local disk (per machine preset); no attachable extra persistent volume API.

volume_shared.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
volume_shared.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no shared-volume feature; state sharing is via your own database/Realtime streams, not a mounted volume.

auto_stop_idle.quote: it sleeps when nobody is typing so you stop paying for it, and wakes on the exact line of code it stopped on
auto_stop_idle.note: Idle chat.agent conversations sleep automatically after an idle timeout (default 30s), and generic waits >=60s checkpoint the run, both unbilled while idle/waiting.

live_resize.quote: The default machine is small-1x which has 0.5 vCPU and 0.5 GB of RAM. You can change the default machine in your trigger.config.ts file
live_resize.note: Machine size (vCPU/RAM preset) is set per task in config or per-trigger override, not changed live on a running instance.

agent_harnesses.quote: MCP server: connect Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, VS Code, Zed, Gemini CLI, etc. to your Trigger.dev project
agent_harnesses.note: Trigger.dev ships an MCP server so external coding-agent harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) can control a Trigger.dev project, but it does not preinstall/offer those harnesses as templates running inside its own sandboxes; its own in-sandbox agent building block is chat.agent (own_agent_api), which you write yourself.

public_ipv4.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
public_ipv4.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — task containers are outbound-only compute triggered by events/API; no inbound public IPv4 per machine (only static outbound IPs per region).

inbound_https.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
inbound_https.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no feature to expose an HTTPS URL that reaches a port on the task's own machine; the only public endpoints are Trigger.dev's own API/webhooks.

ingress_rules.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
ingress_rules.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — no inbound ports are exposed on task machines, so there is nothing to apply ingress access rules to.

egress_allowlist.quote: Reach private databases, caches, and APIs from your tasks over AWS PrivateLink. No public endpoints, no IP allowlists, no VPN.
egress_allowlist.note: Private networking lets tasks reach your private resources via PrivateLink (avoiding the need for you to IP-allowlist Trigger.dev); it is not a provider-side control restricting what a task itself can reach outbound (no documented allow/deny egress list or no-internet mode).

egress_http_rules.quote: Reach private databases, caches, and APIs from your tasks over AWS PrivateLink. No public endpoints, no IP allowlists, no VPN.
egress_http_rules.note: No HTTP method/path-level egress control documented; only static outbound IPs and PrivateLink connectivity to your own resources.

guest_firewall.quote: You can review the build output by running deploy with the --dry-run flag, which will output the Containerfile and the build output.
guest_firewall.note: Isolation is container-based (not a full VM/microVM with root=true), so the guest-firewall-with-root heuristic does not apply; no in-guest nftables/iptables capability is documented.

windows.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
windows.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — a Node.js/Bun-based TypeScript task runtime on Linux containers; no Windows machines offered.

macos.quote: Tasks are functions that can run for a long time and provide strong resilience to failure. They run on our servers so there are no timeouts and no infrastructure to manage.
macos.note: not offered: outside the product's scope — Linux container task runtime only; no macOS machines offered.

arm64.quote: Preset	vCPU	Memory	Disk space micro 0.25 0.25 10GB small-1x (default) 0.5 0.5 10GB small-2x 1 1 10GB medium-1x 1 2 10GB medium-2x 2 4 10GB large-1x 4 8 10GB large-2x 8 16 10GB
arm64.note: Only vCPU/RAM/disk machine presets are documented, with no ARM/architecture option; the fixed presets and AWS-based infra imply x86-64 only.

byoc.quote: Yes. The full stack (dashboard, orchestrator, workers, CLI) is Apache 2.0 and deploys with Docker Compose or Kubernetes. It is the same core codebase as Cloud.
byoc.note: Trigger.dev offers full self-hosting (you deploy and operate the open-source stack yourself), not a provider-managed BYOC deployment into your own cloud account; the managed product (Cloud) runs in Trigger.dev's own AWS accounts/regions.

eu_data_residency.quote: Run your tasks in AWS US West (Oregon). A third region alongside US East and Europe, for low latency to West Coast services and APIs.
eu_data_residency.note: Trigger.dev Cloud has a Europe region (eu-central-1) you can pin task deployment to, alongside US East/US West.

max_session_h.quote: How long can a task run for? Tasks can run for as long as you need, with no timeouts.
max_session_h.note: No maximum single-run execution duration is enforced; a separate 14-day maximum queue TTL applies before a run starts executing, which is a different limit.

persistent_disk.quote: While waiting for a subtask or during a long programmed pause (e.g., `wait.for({ minutes: 5 })`), the system uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace) to create a checkpoint of the task's entire state, including memory, CPU registers, and open file descriptors. ... The checkpoint is loaded back into a new execution environment, restoring the task to its exact state before suspension.
persistent_disk.note: Contradiction confirmed: the card already records pause_resume=true and snapshot_auto=true (CRIU checkpoint) but persistent_disk=false. The CRIU checkpoint captures the run's entire process/filesystem state (memory, CPU registers, open file descriptors), and restoration puts the task back in its exact prior state, so on-disk state written before a wait/pause does survive the pause-resume cycle automatically (default behaviour, no opt-in). Scope is narrower than a general persistent volume: it's per-task-run state preserved only across a checkpoint triggered by triggerAndWait/wait.for/wait.until (>=60s) or chat.agent idling, not a disk you can keep across separate deploys/task invocations or attach/detach at will. Corrected value: persistent_disk=true, with the caveat that it's scoped to a single run's pause/resume lifecycle rather than a durable attachable volume.

gpu.note: Confirmed no evidence gap: the official machine-configuration docs, pricing page, and llms.txt index list only CPU/RAM/disk presets for tasks (a durable-TypeScript-background-jobs platform); there is no GPU preset, GPU pricing, or any mention of 'gpu' anywhere in docs.trigger.dev machines/how-it-works pages or trigger.dev/pricing. Product is plainly CPU-only background job execution, consistent with the existing gpu=false and gpu_types=[] values.

usage_api.quote: Billing and usage information is only accessible through the dashboard; no REST API, SDK method, or CLI command is documented for programmatically querying billable usage per environment, task, or run.
usage_api.note: granularity: account-only; cost: no; Trigger.dev offers Management API for agent sessions and webhook/trigger APIs, but no usage/billing endpoint. Dashboard displays billing status and spend limits, but customers cannot retrieve usage metrics per environment or sandbox programmatically.
